hook.scenario: Your FastAPI app started as a sleek 50-line `main.py`. Six months later, it's a 4,000-line monster. Every time someone adds a route, you get Git merge conflicts. Finding the logic for updating a user profile involves scrolling past 50 unrelated endpoints.
hook.question: How do you split a FastAPI application across multiple files without breaking the routing?

mental_model.intuition: A router is a specialized department in a store. `main.py` is just the store's front door.
mental_model.description: Think of `main.py` as the store directory at the entrance. It doesn't stock the shelves; it just says 'Groceries are down Aisle 1, Electronics are down Aisle 2'. In FastAPI, an `APIRouter` acts as a 'mini-FastAPI' app for a specific department (like users or items). You define routes on the router, and then the main app simply 'includes' the router, pointing traffic to it.

sections.body: When building an API, grouping related endpoints (like all `/users` operations or all `/orders` operations) is crucial for maintainability. If you put everything in one file, it becomes unreadable and causes merge conflicts on a team.
sections.recap: Single-file APIs do not scale to team development.

sections.body: FastAPI provides `APIRouter`, which works exactly like the main `FastAPI` app instance but is designed to be modular. You create an `APIRouter` in a separate file, attach routes to it using `@router.get()` or `@router.post()`, and export it.
sections.recap: An APIRouter is a 'mini-app' that holds a group of related endpoints.

sections.body: In your `main.py`, you wire these modules together using `app.include_router()`. When you include a router, you can assign a common `prefix` (like `/users`) and `tags` (for the OpenAPI docs). This saves you from typing `/users` on every single route in the router file.
sections.recap: The main app imports and includes routers, often applying a common prefix.

sections.body: Because you can apply prefixes at the `include_router` level, the paths inside the router file should be relative to that prefix. If your prefix is `/users`, a route for `/users/{id}` should just be defined as `/{id}` in the router.
sections.recap: Router paths combine with the include prefix to form the final URL.

code_snippets.title: 1. The Router File (routers/users.py)
code_snippets.explanation: We use `APIRouter` instead of `FastAPI`. The paths here (`/` and `/{user_id}`) are intentionally missing the `/users` prefix, making the code more DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).

code_snippets.title: 2. The Main App (main.py)
code_snippets.explanation: The main app acts as a registry. By passing `prefix="/users"`, FastAPI automatically prepends it to every route inside `users.router`. The final URLs become `/users/` and `/users/{user_id}`.

key_points.title: Modularity
key_points.detail: Use APIRouter to break large applications into smaller, manageable files grouped by resource.

key_points.title: Prefixing
key_points.detail: Apply URL prefixes in `include_router` to avoid repeating them on every route definition.

key_points.title: OpenAPI Tags
key_points.detail: Passing `tags` to `include_router` automatically groups all those endpoints together in the /docs UI.

common_mistakes.title: Double prefixing the URL path
common_mistakes.explanation: Setting `prefix="/users"` in `include_router`, but then defining the route as `@router.get("/users/{id}")` inside the router. This results in the URL `/users/users/{id}`.

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting to include the router
common_mistakes.explanation: Creating a beautiful router file with 20 endpoints, but forgetting to call `app.include_router()` in `main.py`. The app will run, but requesting any of those endpoints returns a 404 Not Found.

recall_questions.q: What FastAPI class is used to create a modular group of routes in a separate file?
How do you connect an `APIRouter` to the main FastAPI application?
recall_questions.answer: By calling `app.include_router(my_router)` in the main application file.

recall_questions.q: If you call `app.include_router(items.router, prefix="/items")` and the router has a route `@router.get("/{id}")`, what is the final URL?
You wrote a new router file, but all its endpoints are returning 404 Not Found. What is the most likely oversight?
recall_questions.answer: Forgetting to import the router and call `app.include_router()` in `main.py`.

oa_questions.question: How do you structure a large FastAPI application to prevent `main.py` from becoming an unmaintainable monolith?
oa_questions.answer: Split endpoints by resource into separate files using `APIRouter`. Each file acts as a mini-app (e.g., `users.py`, `orders.py`). Then, import these routers into `main.py` and register them using `app.include_router()`, often applying a common prefix like `/users` to the entire group.

oa_questions.question: A developer adds a router to a FastAPI app with `app.include_router(users_router, prefix="/api/users")`. Inside the router, they define a route as `@router.get("/api/users/profile")`. What bug does this introduce?
oa_questions.answer: Double prefixing. The final URL generated by FastAPI will concatenate them, resulting in `/api/users/api/users/profile`. The route inside the router should just be `@router.get("/profile")`.
